title: DENSE_RANK
description:
DENSE_RANK() OVER (...) also gives tied rows the same rank, but unlike RANK it never leaves a gap afterward - the next distinct value always gets the very next integer. Using the same CTE as the previous exercise, write a query that returns each department's `department_id`, `emp_count`, and its DENSE_RANK by emp_count (most staffed first, empty departments included).

WITH dept_counts AS (
    SELECT departments.id AS department_id, COUNT(employees.id) AS emp_count
    FROM departments
    LEFT JOIN employees ON departments.id = employees.department_id
    GROUP BY departments.id
)
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: DENSE_RANK, ties

Compare this to the RANK exercise: the departments tied at 2 employees still share a rank, and so do the ones tied at 0 - but here each new distinct emp_count gets the very next integer, with no rank number ever skipped.
WITH dept_counts AS (...) SELECT department_id, emp_count, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY emp_count DESC) AS emp_rank FROM dept_counts.
expected_behavior: Returns department_id, emp_count, and a DENSE_RANK where tied emp_count values share a rank and no rank number is ever skipped.
solution: WITH dept_counts AS (SELECT departments.id AS department_id, COUNT(employees.id) AS emp_count FROM departments LEFT JOIN employees ON departments.id = employees.department_id GROUP BY departments.id) SELECT department_id, emp_count, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY emp_count DESC) AS emp_rank FROM dept_counts;
explanation: RANK and DENSE_RANK agree completely when there are no ties - they only diverge the moment two rows share a value, which is exactly why this dataset was built with real ties in it (at 2 employees, and again at 0).
